context: road systems · ducts and foundations with the road, equipment late, integration with the traffic control centre

brief.intro: New to this project type? Traffic signals and intelligent transport systems (ITS) are the electronics of a road: signal heads and controllers at junctions, detectors in or above the road, CCTV, variable message signs, speed and red-light enforcement, and the fibre network that links them all to a traffic control centre. Like street lighting, the civil part — ducts, chambers, pole and gantry foundations — is built into the road works early. The equipment arrives late and installs quickly. The real finishing work is software and integration: each junction's timings are configured and tested, every device must talk to the control centre, and the traffic authority must witness the tests before a junction is switched on.

glossary.plain: the computer in the roadside cabinet that runs the signal timings of a junction.
a group of movements that get green together, and the order in which they run.
a wire loop cut into the road that senses vehicles; it can only be cut after the asphalt is laid.
variable message sign — an electronic sign that shows messages to drivers.
the steel structure spanning or reaching over the road that carries signs or signals.
factory acceptance test and site acceptance test — the two formal tests of the equipment.
a safety test proving the controller can never show conflicting greens.
the traffic management centre and its software that monitors and controls the devices.

must_get_right: Ducts, chambers and foundations go in with the road works; gantry foundations are substantial structures and need to be in the road contractor's sequence early.
Loop detectors are cut after the final asphalt and before road marking — a narrow window; above-ground detectors avoid it.
Power supply to each controller cabinet and the fibre link to the control centre are prerequisites for any testing.
Give integration real time: controller configuration, site acceptance tests and the authority's witnessed switch-on for each junction, plus a period of monitoring.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by junction and by road section for the mid-block systems, so each junction can be read from civil works to switch-on.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar; gantry erection and work on live junctions are night or weekend activities under road closures. Switch-on dates are agreed with the traffic authority and police.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Ducts and foundations with the road works → poles and gantries → cabling → equipment → power and communications → configuration → SAT → integration → switch-on. Loops are tied to the final asphalt. The critical path runs through equipment delivery after FAT, or through the last junction released by the road works.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The road contractor provides ducts and foundations in sequence; power is available at each cabinet; the control centre is ready to accept new devices; the authority attends FAT, SAT and switch-on within the assumed notice.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Work at live junctions needs traffic management and police approval; road closures for gantries are limited in number and length.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late approval of junction design, missed ducts, late power, software integration problems with the control centre, and authority comments at switch-on. Contingency is held before the road-opening date.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by junction and system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the civil, cabling and installation teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
